name: Noise Pop
about: Noise pop pairs sweet, simple songwriting with walls of distortion and feedback, and its founding document is the Jesus and Mary Chain's Psychocandy from 1985, which took the Velvet Underground and the Shangri-Las as twin models. The template is a girl-group or bubblegum melody, a buried or deadpan vocal, and guitars treated as weather rather than lead instruments; the drums are often rudimentary and the production deliberately cheap. Dinosaur Jr. and My Bloody Valentine pushed the guitars louder and stranger, Yo La Tengo and the Vaselines kept the songs in front, and a 2000s revival around the Raveonettes, Deerhunter, No Age and the Pains of Being Pure at Heart made fuzz and reverb the default setting for a generation of American indie bands, where it remains.

artists.name: The Jesus and Mary Chain
artists.why: feedback over girl-group melodies, the template

artists.name: The Raveonettes
artists.why: Danish duo who revived the formula

artists.name: Deerhunter
artists.why: made the fuzz dreamlike and strange

artists.name: The Pains of Being Pure at Heart
A Place to Bury Strangers
artists.why: the loudest band in New York

albums.title: Psychocandy
albums.why: The Reid brothers bury Phil Spector melodies under sheets of feedback and invent a genre in forty minutes, still the record every noise pop band answers to.

albums.title: Darklands
albums.why: The feedback is dialled back and the songs stand exposed, proving the brothers' tunes were always the point; Just Like Honey's sequel in black.

albums.title: Isn't Anything
albums.why: The record where Kevin Shields found the bent, glided guitar sound, with pop songs still visible underneath before Loveless dissolved them entirely.

albums.title: You're Living All Over Me
albums.why: J Mascis's ear-splitting volume and slacker drawl carry some of the decade's best indie songwriting; Lou Barlow's bass fights it the whole way.

albums.title: Lovely
albums.why: Coventry's answer to the Mary Chain and Blondie, carried by Crash and Tracy Tracy's bright vocals over scuffed, fast guitars.

albums.title: Dum-Dum
albums.why: Eugene Kelly and Frances McKee's only original album is crude, funny and tuneful, and became scripture once Nirvana started covering it.

albums.title: A Catholic Education
albums.why: Before the harmonies were polished, the Fanclub were a Dinosaur Jr.-indebted fuzz band, and this ragged debut shows the songs already forming.

albums.title: Black Tambourine
albums.why: The complete recordings of the Maryland band whose handful of singles defined the American twee-noise axis and seeded the entire Slumberland label.

albums.title: Shot Forth Self Living
albums.why: Brad Laner's Los Angeles band were America's harshest shoegazers, with treble-shredded guitars around Beth Thompson's placid pop vocals.

albums.title: Copacetic
albums.why: The Sub Pop debut that pointed the label away from grunge, all jangle and fuzz under Sarah Shannon's clear, unbothered singing.

albums.title: Painful
albums.why: The album where Yo La Tengo became themselves, balancing organ-drone lullabies against long feedback squalls with new patience and warmth.

albums.title: Blonder Tongue Audio Baton
albums.why: Boston's answer to Loveless splices tape experiments and tape hiss between genuinely lovely songs; a cult record that has only grown.

albums.title: Chain Gang of Love
albums.why: Written entirely in B flat major, the Danish duo's debut album is a sleek, knowing restatement of Psychocandy with Everly Brothers harmonies.

albums.title: A Place to Bury Strangers
albums.why: Oliver Ackermann's pedal-building obsession produces the most punishing noise pop debut of its decade, with Mary Chain melodies barely audible underneath.

albums.title: Microcastle
albums.why: Bradford Cox's Atlanta band pull dreamy, damaged pop out of ambient drift and garage fuzz; the most influential American indie record of its year.

albums.title: Nouns
albums.why: The Smell's house band condense punk urgency and ambient haze into thirty minutes that sound like skateboarding through a sampler.

albums.title: Rip It Off
albums.why: Columbus's trio recorded their Matador debut so far into the red that the hooks have to be reconstructed from the distortion, which is the fun of it.

albums.title: Vivian Girls
albums.why: Twenty-two minutes of Brooklyn reverb, three-part harmonies and Black Tambourine worship that set off a wave of lo-fi girl-group revivalists.

albums.title: Alight of Night
albums.why: Brad Hargett's cavernous baritone and Velvets-via-Mary Chain drone make a cold, elegant Brooklyn debut that nods more than it rocks.

albums.artist: The Pains of Being Pure at Heart
albums.title: The Pains of Being Pure at Heart
albums.why: A debut that reassembles the Field Mice, Black Tambourine and My Bloody Valentine with such affection and craft that the borrowing stops mattering.

albums.title: Treats
albums.why: Derek Miller's clipping, overdriven riffs and Alexis Krauss's cheerleader chants make the loudest pop record of 2010, built for distortion on earbuds.

albums.title: King of the Beach
albums.why: Nathan Williams trades bedroom hiss for a real studio and delivers bratty, sun-damaged surf-punk songs that justify the earlier hype.

albums.title: I Will Be
albums.why: Dee Dee Penny's debut proper runs Mary Chain fuzz through girl-group songcraft with Richard Gottehrer, a Blondie producer, keeping it crisp.

albums.title: Yuck
albums.why: A London band's loving reconstruction of 1990s American college rock, from Dinosaur Jr. riffs to Yo La Tengo hush, with better songs than the pastiche implies.
